title: Scheduler Resource Tagging and Precedence Manifest
author: Asha Patel
body:
Overview

Purpose: This document specifies the resource-tagging and precedence manifest used by Redwood's scheduler to make deterministic decisions about kernel assignment, admission control, and graceful degradation. Resource tags let higher layers add lightweight metadata to requests (workload characteristics, cost-sensitivity, fidelity budget, retry semantics) that the scheduler uses together with telemetry to make per-request placement and preemption choices.

Goals
- Make scheduling decisions predictable and auditable by standardizing tags and precedence rules.
- Expose controllable levers to product and platform teams to express cost vs fidelity tradeoffs.
- Ensure backward compatibility: untagged requests follow current best-effort policies.
- Provide operator runbooks and profiling guidance for tag-driven regressions.

Scope and Non-Goals
- Scope: runtime admission controller, scheduler policy layer, kernel hinting, and observability fields.
- Non-Goals: model selection logic, API surface changes for customers (tags are internal to Redwood and derived from routing policies or per-tenant config).

Key Concepts and Terminology
- Resource Tag: structured label attached to a request at the service boundary. Tags are short key:value tokens.
- Precedence Manifest: ordered rule set that maps tag combinations to scheduling actions (admit, queue-with-sla, degrade-mode, preemptible).
- Degradation Mode: a policy action that reduces fidelity (quantized model variant, prefix cache usage, early cutoff).
- Kernel Hint: annotation passed to kernel mapper that influences kernel selection (e.g., preferred kernel family or tight latency bound).

Design Principles
1) Keep tags small and typed: allow exactly the tag keys documented in the manifest.
2) Deterministic precedence: rules are evaluated top-to-bottom; earlier rule wins.
3) Least-privilege impact: tags can only reduce resource footprint or request priority, never increase allocation.
4) Observability-first: every evaluation emits a traceable event containing the matched rule id and rationale.

Resource Tag Schema (canonical keys)
- fidelity: {high, standard, economical}  # fidelity budget for the request
- cost_sensitivity: {low, medium, high}  # willingness to use expensive kernels or CPU fallback
- latency_class: {interactive, best_effort, batch}  # latency tolerance
- preemptible: {true, false}  # candidate for preemption under pressure
- cache_hint: {kv_prefetch, prefix_cache_ok, no_cache}  # cache preferences
- isolation: {tenant_dedicated, tenant_shared}  # tenancy isolation; impacts shard placement

Example Tagging Table (ascii)
| Tag key | Purpose | Default | Notes |
| fidelity | fidelity budget | standard | high=use highest-quality model variant if latency allows |
| cost_sensitivity | operator cost tolerance | medium | low=prefer quantized kernels and batching |
| latency_class | scheduling latency target | interactive | impacts admission timeout |
| preemptible | preemption candidacy | false | true allows background eviction under pressure |

Precedence Manifest (human-readable sample)
1) rule_id: P-01-critical-interactive
   match: fidelity=high AND latency_class=interactive AND isolation=tenant_dedicated
   action: admit_prefetch, kernel_hint=low-latency, preemptible=false
   rationale: SLA-backed dedicated tenant traffic must be prioritized; kernel hint prefers kernels tuned for short sequences

2) rule_id: P-02-econ-background
   match: fidelity=economical OR cost_sensitivity=high OR preemptible=true
   action: queue-with-sla(200ms), kernel_hint=quantized-prefer, allow_batched_execution=true
   rationale: background tasks should use cost-optimized paths and accept higher latency

3) rule_id: P-03-standard-shared
   match: isolation=tenant_shared AND latency_class=interactive
   action: admit_with_quota, kernel_hint=balanced, preemptible=true

4) rule_id: P-99-default
   match: catch-all
   action: best-effort admit, kernel_hint=balanced

Manifest Format and Storage
- Manifest is stored as a versioned YAML in the control plane: /manifests/scheduler/resource-precedence/{version}.yaml
- Each manifest publishes: id, created_by, created_at, rules[], validation_hash.
- Validation: control plane runs static validation on update (no contradictory rules, explicit default rule present).

YAML Example (extracted)
---
version: v1.2
created_by: scheduler-team
created_at: 2026-02-01
rules:
  - id: P-01-critical-interactive
    match: "fidelity == 'high' && latency_class == 'interactive' && isolation == 'tenant_dedicated'"
    action: "admit_prefetch, kernel_hint=low-latency, preemptible=false"
  - id: P-02-econ-background
    match: "fidelity == 'economical' || cost_sensitivity == 'high' || preemptible == 'true'"
    action: "queue-with-sla(200ms), kernel_hint=quantized-prefer, allow_batched_execution=true"
---

Runtime Evaluation Flow (per-request)
1) Request enters ingress; routing layer attaches derived tags (from customer config, route labels, or system defaults).
2) Admission controller fetches latest precedence manifest and evaluates rules top-to-bottom.
3) Matched action produces an Admission Decision object containing: target kernel_hint, admission_bucket, preemptible flag, degradation plan id.
4) Admission decision is persisted as an event and attached to the request trace for auditing.
5) Kernel mapper consumes kernel_hint and schedules kernel execution; preemption decisions are handled by the quota controller.

Observability and Telemetry Changes
- New telemetry fields to include in traces/metrics: precedent_rule_id, admission_decision, computed_slot_cost_estimate, kernel_hint, preemptible_flag.
- Exported metrics: precedence_rule_match_count{rule_id}, precedence_rule_latency_ms{rule_id}.
- Alerting: sudden shift in matches to P-02-econ-background for a high-SLA tenant triggers an incident.

Profiling and Benchmarking Guidance
- Profiling playbook change: when benchmarking slot consumption, record matched precedence_rule_id for each trace. Use this to correlate rule effects on tail latency.
- New microbench: tag-sensitivity-stressor. Procedure:
  1) Generate synthetic traffic with identical payloads but differing tag sets (high vs economical).
  2) Measure kernel selection distribution, per-token latency, and per-request cost.
  3) Validate that economical tags reduce per-token cost by >= 20% vs standard baseline for same model family.

Operator Runbook: Precedence Regression (critical)
- Symptom: production latency spike coinciding with increased matches to P-02-econ-background for interactive routes.
- Quick triage steps:
  1) Query traces for precedence_rule_match_count where rule_id==P-02-econ-background over last 15m.
     CLI: rquery metrics precedence_rule_match_count --filter "rule_id=P-02-econ-background" --range 15m
  2) Identify affected tenant_ids from traces with tag isolation=tenant_shared and latency_class=interactive.
  3) Roll back manifest to previous version: control-plane-cli manifest rollback --name resource-precedence --to-version v1.1
  4) If rollback not possible, apply emergency override: control-plane-cli manifest patch --set "rules[0].action='admit_with_quota, kernel_hint=balanced, preemptible=false'"
  5) Post-incident: run profiling microbench and annotate the root cause in the incident ticket.

Release Notes (short entry)
- 2026-06-15: Introduced Resource Tagging & Precedence Manifest v1.2.0.
  - Adds fidelity/cost_sensitivity/latency_class tags.
  - Default manifest contains deterministic precedence and observability hooks.
  - Telemetry fields added: precedent_rule_id, kernel_hint.

Backward Compatibility and Migration
- Untagged traffic is matched by P-99-default and behaves like existing scheduler logic.
- Migration plan for Dedicated customers: gradually attach isolation=tenant_dedicated at routing-layer; this unlocks lower-latency kernels and disables preemption.

Security and Privacy Considerations
- Tags contain no PII and are generated by routing logic or internal policy.
- Manifest changes are restricted to scheduler-admin role with audit logging enabled.

Known Limitations and Issues
- K-101: Under multi-tenant noise, the "queue-with-sla(200ms)" action can lead to unpredictable slot entanglement. Mitigation: add explicit per-tenant queue caps in next manifest.
- K-102: Kernel_hint favors quantized kernels for economical tags; regression found on short-sequence chat where quantized kernel introduces hallucination regressions under specific logits threshold. Tracking ticket: SCHED-4793.

Testing and Validation Checklist for Manifest Changes
1) Static validation: lint manifest, ensure default rule present.
2) Unit tests: rule matching semantics, short-circuit precedence ordering tests.
3) Integration canary: deploy to canary pool for non-critical tenants for 48h.
4) Benchmark gate: run tag-sensitivity-stressor and verify cost/latency deltas against baseline.
5) Beta rollout: enable for 10% traffic of new tenants, monitor precedence_rule_match_count and tail latency.

Operational Metrics to Monitor After Rollout
- precedence_rule_match_count by rule_id (trend and sudden shifts)
- admission_decision_latencies P50/P90/P99
- kernel_selection_entropy (higher indicates varied kernel churn)
- per-tenant preemptions per-minute

Owner and Contact
- Primary owner: eng-serving-scheduler team (oncall alias: eng-serving-scheduler@redwood.ai)
- Document steward: Asha Patel (asha.patel@redwood.ai)

Appendix A: Example Trace Snippet (annotated)
- trace_id: 0001
- tags: fidelity=high, latency_class=interactive, isolation=tenant_dedicated
- precedence_rule_id: P-01-critical-interactive
- admission_decision: admit_prefetch; kernel_hint=low-latency; preemptible=false
- kernel_selected: kernel-family-v2-lowlatency

Appendix B: FAQ
Q: Can customers influence tags?
A: Not directly. Tags are derived from routing rules and customer's plan mapping (dedicated vs shared, SLAs), and from internal cost-sensitivity mappings.

Q: Will tags slow down admission?
A: Tag matching is optimized and cached per route; additional latency is under 200us in canary measurements.
